item.title: Replacing a k3s Cluster With One ePHPm Process
item.description:
A couple of weeks ago I wrote up surviving a node rebuild on single-node k3s. Put the stateful bytes on a dedicated EBS volume, treat the node as cattle, and rebuild the machine without losing the data. It works.

Then I looked at what I was actually running on that node and felt a little silly.

The workload is three PHP sites (an admin app, self-hosted Sendy for email, a wholesale catalog) plus three crons. That’s it. To run it I had a k3s control plane, a kubelet, Traefik for ingress, Tailscale for access, a CSI driver, a litestream sidecar for backups, three k8s CronJobs, and a stack of Helm charts holding it together. Every piece of that is something I patch, monitor, and get paged for, and none of it is the app. It was a datacenter wrapped around three PHP sites and some crons.

item.title: Operating the One-Box ePHPm Setup: Backups and Blue/Green
item.description:
The golden AMI: immutable code, mutable data

The box is baked, not configured in place. Packer builds a Debian 12 AMI with the ePHPm binary and all three apps’ code already on disk. The source gets pulled from the three private GitHub repos’ tarballs at build time and run through composer install right there in the image. Rolling new code means baking a new AMI.

Debian 12 specifically, because the admin app’s imagick build is compiled against glibc 2.36 and bookworm is that exact version. (That ABI pin is also why the box stayed on AWS amd64 instead of chasing a free ARM tier. That’s the cost math in part one.)

item.title: Dagger on ephemerd, and a Warm Cache on Throwaway Runners
item.description:
A friend asked me whether Dagger replaces ephemerd. It doesn’t — they sit at different layers, and I wrote half this post explaining that before I noticed the more interesting question hiding underneath it.

Ephemeral runners throw the whole machine away after every job. That is deliberate: a fork PR gets a clean, single-use box and nothing it does survives. But the build cache does not survive either. Every job starts cold — re-pull the base images, recompile from scratch, re-download every dependency. The usual fix is a long-running build engine with a persistent disk, which for a hardened fleet means standing up a privileged box that sits outside your isolation. That trade bothered me enough to measure the alternative.

item.title: Surviving a Node Rebuild: A Durable ePHPm Blog on Single-Node k3s
item.description:
A single ePHPm binary runs a whole WordPress site. No php-fpm, no Redis, no MySQL. The database is a SQLite file. I covered that setup in Zero-Dependency Deployments. It makes for a tiny blog: one process, one file, a distroless image around 270 MB. That fits a micro VM with room to spare.

So I put one on a micro EC2 instance with single-node k3s. One box, one kubectl, no control-plane sprawl. You create a PersistentVolumeClaim, the blog binds to it, and it looks like your data is safe.

item.title: Docker-in-Docker in CI Without Handing Jobs Root
item.description:
ephemerd runs a fresh GitHub Actions runner per job. Some of those jobs need Docker. A workflow builds an image, runs a service container, or uses the container: key. The usual way to give a self-hosted job Docker is Docker-in-Docker, or dind.

The catch is what dind normally costs you. The standard recipe is a --privileged container. Privileged hands the job most of root on the host. For CI that runs fork pull requests, that is a non-starter. A fork PR is a stranger’s code.

item.title: Cache Proxies for Ephemeral CI Runners
item.description:
ephemerd gives every CI job a brand new runner. A new container on Linux, a new VM on macOS and Windows. The job runs, the runner is thrown away, and the next job starts from a clean image. That is the whole point. Nothing a job does can leak into the next one.

Clean has a cost. A fresh runner has an empty cache. So every job downloads the world again. Go modules, crates, the Rust toolchain, Composer packages, release tarballs. On a busy repo that is gigabytes a day, pulled over and over, most of it byte-for-byte identical to what the last job pulled.

item.title: Cross-Platform Process Containment: Job Objects vs Process Groups vs cgroups
item.description: Every turn a shipmates crew member takes is a subprocess. It’s claude or the codex app-server. That in turn spawns shells, go test, npm or whatever the task calls for. Two things have to be true about that tree. When a turn ends or gets killed, the whole tree goes, including the grandchildren. And if somebody sets a memory or CPU budget, the budget applies to the whole tree, not just the process I happened to start.

item.title: Bind Mounts Across Mount Namespaces: Four PRs and a Container Escape
item.description: GitHub Actions has a container: key that runs a job’s steps inside an image of your choosing. It’s popular because it gives you a reproducible toolchain without building a custom runner image. On a self-hosted runner it works by having the runner drive Docker. On ephemerd, “Docker” is a shim that speaks the Docker API and creates containers in containerd. Getting bind mounts right through that shim took four PRs in a week. A couple of months later the version that worked turned out to be an escape.

item.title: Zero-Dependency Deployments - Single Binary for WordPress
item.description:
The standard way to run a WordPress site is four services:

  • nginx for HTTP and TLS
  • php-fpm to run PHP
  • MySQL for data
  • Redis, once the site gets slow enough that someone installs an object cache plugin

That’s four processes and four config files. There are three sockets between them and four things to upgrade. For a big site that’s fine. For a brochure site or a staging copy it’s absurd. The same goes for a PR preview, a box at the edge, or a CI job that needs a real WordPress to test a plugin against.

item.title: Kata Containers for CI: Boot Cost Isn't the Problem, File I/O Is
item.description: Of the three platforms ephemerd runs jobs on, Linux has the weakest isolation. Windows jobs get a Hyper-V isolated container with its own kernel. macOS jobs get a whole VM. A Linux job is an ordinary runc container sharing the host kernel. A kernel escape from a Linux job is a host compromise. Kata Containers fixes that by putting each container in a lightweight VM with its own kernel. It plugs into containerd as just another runtime handler. So I added it in #155, measured it, and left it off by default. This post is why.

item.title: Per-Tenant Network Policy in One Process: ePHPm's eBPF Thread Tags
item.description:
In multi-tenant mode ePHPm serves every site in sites_dir from one process. Every tenant’s PHP runs as the same OS user on the same pool of ZTS threads. A thread that just served blog.example will serve shop.example a few milliseconds later. That’s the density win. It also means the kernel has no idea which tenant is behind a given connect(). As far as Linux is concerned it’s all ephpm-web.

Most of the isolation work in ePHPm happens above the kernel. That covers open_basedir, the function denylist, per-site databases and KV keyspaces. Network is the one place where that isn’t enough. This week we brought eBPF in to give the kernel a per-tenant identity. It went from a roadmap doc on Wednesday morning to merged that evening (#413, aimed at v0.8.1). v0.8.1 never got a release because its Linux legs failed to link. v0.8.2 shipped with the BPF object silently stubbed out. v0.8.3 was the first release that carried it. This post covers what it enforces and what it costs. It also covers what broke on the way out the door and what it doesn’t do.

item.title: My iptables Rule Matched 0 Packets in 9.8 GB
item.description:
After a week of Windows firewall rules that listed fine and enforced nothing, I went back to the Linux side of ephemerd feeling pretty good about it. iptables is the boring, well-understood one. item.title: ephemerd: One Daemon, a Fresh Runner Per Job, Every OS
item.description: I have CI that needs Linux amd64, Linux arm64, Windows and macOS. GitHub-hosted runners for all four get expensive fast, especially the arm64 and Mac minutes. Self-hosted runners fix the bill and create a different problem. A stock actions/runner on a box you own runs whatever the workflow says. It keeps whatever the last job left behind. And it’s one fork PR away from somebody running code on your LAN.
